claim: Glioblastomas (GBM) are aggressive and therapy-resistant brain tumours.
source: Glioblastomas (GBM) are aggressive and therapy-resistant brain tumours, which contain a subpopulation of tumour-propagating glioblastoma stem-like cells (GSC) thought to drive progression and recurrence.
evidence: This is a well-established characterization of GBM in the scientific literature.

claim: GBM contain a subpopulation of tumour-propagating glioblastoma stem-like cells (GSC) thought to drive progression and recurrence.
source: Glioblastomas (GBM) are aggressive and therapy-resistant brain tumours, which contain a subpopulation of tumour-propagating glioblastoma stem-like cells (GSC) thought to drive progression and recurrence.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations in the introduction and represents established knowledge in the field.

claim: Diffuse invasion of the brain parenchyma, including along preexisting blood vessels, is a leading cause of therapeutic resistance in GBM.
source: Diffuse invasion of the brain parenchyma, including along preexisting blood vessels, is a leading cause of therapeutic resistance, but the mechanisms remain unclear.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the abstract and is supported by citations in the introduction.

claim: Ephrin-B2 mediates GSC perivascular invasion.
source: Here, we show that ephrin-B2 mediates GSC perivascular invasion.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by intravital imaging and mechanistic studies described in the manuscript.

claim: Endothelial ephrin-B2 compartmentalises non-tumourigenic cells.
source: Intravital imaging, coupled with mechanistic studies in murine GBM models and patient-derived GSC, revealed that endothelial ephrin-B2 compartmentalises non-tumourigenic cells.
evidence: This finding is supported by intravital imaging experiments and in vitro migration assays shown in Figure 1.

claim: Upregulation of ephrin-B2 ligand in GSC enables perivascular migration through homotypic forward signalling.
source: In contrast, upregulation of the same ephrin-B2 ligand in GSC enabled perivascular migration through homotypic forward signalling.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing that ephrin-B2 overexpression in imNSC enables migration and that this depends on forward signaling.

claim: Ephrin-B2 reverse signalling promotes tumourigenesis cell-autonomously by mediating anchorage-independent cytokinesis via RhoA.
source: Surprisingly, ephrin-B2 reverse signalling also promoted tumourigenesis cell-autonomously, by mediating anchorage-independent cytokinesis via RhoA.
evidence: This is supported by soft agar assays, cell cycle analysis, and RhoA activation experiments shown in Figures 4 and 5.

claim: EFNB2 knock-down in human GSC-derived orthotopic xenografts blocks tumour initiation.
source: In human GSC-derived orthotopic xenografts, EFNB2 knock-down blocked tumour initiation and treatment of established tumours with ephrin-B2-blocking antibodies suppressed progression.
evidence: This is supported by in vivo tumourigenicity studies with shEFNB2 human GSC shown in Figure 7.

claim: Treatment of established tumours with ephrin-B2-blocking antibodies suppresses progression.
source: In human GSC-derived orthotopic xenografts, EFNB2 knock-down blocked tumour initiation and treatment of established tumours with ephrin-B2-blocking antibodies suppressed progression.
evidence: This is supported by in vivo experiments with B11 antibody treatment shown in Figure 8.

claim: Targeting ephrin-B2 may be an effective strategy for the simultaneous inhibition of invasion and proliferation in GBM.
source: Thus, our results indicate that targeting ephrin-B2 may be an effective strategy for the simultaneous inhibition of invasion and proliferation in GBM.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data showing ephrin-B2's dual roles in invasion and proliferation.

claim: GBM is the most common and aggressive type of primary brain tumour.
source: Glioblastoma (GBM) is the most common and aggressive type of primary brain tumour and one of the most lethal types of cancer (Chen et al., 2012b).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Chen et al., 2012b.

claim: Current GBM therapies consist of maximally safe surgical resection followed by radio and chemotherapy.
source: Current therapies consist of maximally safe surgical resection followed by radio and chemotherapy.
evidence: This is established clinical knowledge about GBM treatment.

claim: Current GBM therapies are largely ineffective and GBM invariably recur following treatment.
source: However, these are largely ineffective and GBM invariably recur following treatment, resulting in a median survival of <15 months (Weathers and Gilbert, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Weathers and Gilbert, 2014.

claim: GBM has a median survival of less than 15 months.
source: However, these are largely ineffective and GBM invariably recur following treatment, resulting in a median survival of <15 months (Weathers and Gilbert, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Weathers and Gilbert, 2014.

claim: Diffuse infiltration of tumour cells into the surrounding brain parenchyma limits efficacy of surgery and radiotherapy.
source: A leading cause of GBM recurrence is the diffuse infiltration of the tumour cells into the surrounding brain parenchyma, which limits efficacy of surgery and radiotherapy (Cuddapah et al., 2014; Lamszus et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Cuddapah et al., 2014 and Lamszus et al., 2003.

claim: GSC are able to self-renew, differentiate into tumour-bulk cells and reconstitute a phenocopy of the original lesion upon transplantation.
source: GBM contain subpopulations of cells with stem cell properties termed glioblastoma stem-like cells (GSC), which are able to self-renew, differentiate into tumour-bulk cells and reconstitute a phenocopy of the original lesion upon transplantation (Venere et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Venere et al., 2011.

claim: GSC are critical players in tumour initiation and progression.
source: It is therefore increasingly recognized that GSC are critical players in tumour initiation and progression.
evidence: This is stated as an increasingly recognized concept in the field.

claim: GSC are intrinsically resistant to chemo- and radiotherapy.
source: Furthermore, GSC were shown to be intrinsically resistant to chemo- and radiotherapy and more invasive than non-stem tumour cells (Chen et al., 2012a; Cheng et al., 2011; Bao et al., 2006; Venere et al., 2011; Sadahiro et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations: Chen et al., 2012a; Cheng et al., 2011; Bao et al., 2006; Venere et al., 2011; Sadahiro et al., 2014.

claim: GSC are more invasive than non-stem tumour cells.
source: Furthermore, GSC were shown to be intrinsically resistant to chemo- and radiotherapy and more invasive than non-stem tumour cells (Chen et al., 2012a; Cheng et al., 2011; Bao et al., 2006; Venere et al., 2011; Sadahiro et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations: Chen et al., 2012a; Cheng et al., 2011; Bao et al., 2006; Venere et al., 2011; Sadahiro et al., 2014.

claim: GSC might be the primary cells within GBM responsible for infiltration and tumour recurrence following therapy.
source: This suggests that GSC might be the primary cells within GBM responsible for infiltration and tumour recurrence following therapy and that GSC-targeting therapies should be beneficial for GBM treatment.
evidence: This is an inference based on the properties of GSC described in the preceding sentences.

claim: GBM invasion occurs along three main routes: the white matter tracts, the interstitial space of the brain and the perivascular space surrounding blood vessels.
source: GBM invasion occurs along three main routes: the white matter tracts, the interstitial space of the brain and the perivascular space surrounding blood vessels (Scherer, 1938; Cuddapah et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Scherer, 1938 and Cuddapah et al., 2014.

claim: Invasion along the perivascular space is a favourable migration route because endothelial cells secrete chemoattractants.
source: Invasion along the perivascular space is a favourable migration route because endothelial cells secrete chemoattractants, which actively recruit tumour cells to the vasculature (Montana and Sontheimer, 2011; Cuddapah et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Montana and Sontheimer, 2011 and Cuddapah et al., 2014.

claim: The perivascular space is enriched in migration-promoting ECM components and is fluid-filled, thereby opposing little physical resistance to invading tumour cells.
source: In addition, the perivascular space is enriched in migration-promoting ECM components and is fluid-filled, thereby opposing little physical resistance to invading tumour cells (Gritsenko et al., 2012; Cuddapah et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Gritsenko et al., 2012 and Cuddapah et al., 2014.

claim: GSC are particularly prone to perivascular invasion due to their similarities with normal neural progenitors.
source: Importantly, within GBM, GSC are particularly prone to perivascular invasion, likely due to their similarities with normal neural progenitors, which preferentially migrate along blood vessels during development and after injury in the adult (Cuddapah et al., 2014; Watkins et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Cuddapah et al., 2014 and Watkins et al., 2014.

claim: GSC reside in perivascular niches.
source: In agreement with this, GSC reside in perivascular niches and the majority of invading cells migrate along the host vasculature in xenograft GSC models of both mouse and human origin (Farin et al., 2006; Zagzag et al., 2008; Baker et al., 2014; Calabrese et al., 2007; Winkler et al., 2009; Watkins et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations: Farin et al., 2006; Zagzag et al., 2008; Baker et al., 2014; Calabrese et al., 2007; Winkler et al., 2009; Watkins et al., 2014.

claim: The majority of invading cells migrate along the host vasculature in xenograft GSC models of both mouse and human origin.
source: In agreement with this, GSC reside in perivascular niches and the majority of invading cells migrate along the host vasculature in xenograft GSC models of both mouse and human origin (Farin et al., 2006; Zagzag et al., 2008; Baker et al., 2014; Calabrese et al., 2007; Winkler et al., 2009; Watkins et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations: Farin et al., 2006; Zagzag et al., 2008; Baker et al., 2014; Calabrese et al., 2007; Winkler et al., 2009; Watkins et al., 2014.

claim: Vascular co-option is an important tumour vascularisation mechanism by which tumours gain access to oxygen and nutrients independent of angiogenesis.
source: First, tumour cell migration along pre-existing normal blood vessels is an important tumour vascularisation mechanism, known as vascular co-option, by which tumours gain access to oxygen and nutrients independent of angiogenesis (Donnem et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Donnem et al., 2013.

claim: Vascular co-option plays crucial roles during initial tumour growth, seeding of satellite lesions and tumour recurrence following therapy.
source: Vascular co-option plays crucial roles during initial tumour growth, seeding of satellite lesions and tumour recurrence following therapy.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge following the citation about vascular co-option.

claim: Association with the perivascular niche provides GSC with important self-renewal and survival signals.
source: Second, association with the perivascular niche provides GSC with important self-renewal and survival signals, which support GSC tumour-propagating abilities and therapeutic resistance (Charles and Holland, 2010).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Charles and Holland, 2010.

claim: GSC share many properties with normal neural stem cells (NSC), such as stem cell markers expression and multilineage differentiation.
source: GSC share many properties with normal neural stem cells (NSC), such as stem cell markers expression (Sox2, Nestin, CD133, ALDH1, etc.) and multilineage differentiation and, importantly, extensive evidence indicates that NSC themselves can be cells of origin in GBM (Chen et al., 2012b; Venere et al., 2011; Chen et al., 2012a).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Chen et al., 2012b; Venere et al., 2011; Chen et al., 2012a.

claim: NSC can be cells of origin in GBM.
source: GSC share many properties with normal neural stem cells (NSC), such as stem cell markers expression (Sox2, Nestin, CD133, ALDH1, etc.) and multilineage differentiation and, importantly, extensive evidence indicates that NSC themselves can be cells of origin in GBM (Chen et al., 2012b; Venere et al., 2011; Chen et al., 2012a).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Chen et al., 2012b; Venere et al., 2011; Chen et al., 2012a.

claim: GSC harbour transforming mutations that drive their tumourigenic properties, including deregulated proliferation and increased invasiveness.
source: However, GSC also significantly differ from their normal counterparts, in that they harbour transforming mutations that drive their tumourigenic properties, including deregulated proliferation and increased invasiveness (Engstrom et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Engstrom et al., 2012.

claim: The authors generated a murine GBM model by sequentially introducing oncogenic lesions relevant to the human disease into normal NSC.
source: In this study, we generated a murine GBM model by sequentially introducing oncogenic lesions relevant to the human disease into normal NSC and compared vascular interactions of the resultant transformed GSC-like cells and immortalised parental cells to interrogate mechanisms of perivascular invasion.
evidence: This describes the experimental approach used in the study.

claim: Ephrin-B2 is a member of the Eph/ephrin family of receptor tyrosine kinases and their membrane-bound ligands.
source: ephrin-B2 is a member of the Eph/ephrin family of receptor tyrosine kinases and their membrane-bound ligands, a fundamental cell communication system with widespread roles in tissue development, maintenance and disease (Pasquale, 2010).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Pasquale, 2010.

claim: Activation of Eph receptors by ephrin ligands on adjacent cells modulates cell behaviour, including migration, proliferation and stemness.
source: Activation of Eph receptors by ephrin ligands on adjacent cells modulates cell behaviour, including migration, proliferation and stemness, by eliciting forward signalling downstream of Ephs and reverse signalling downstream of ephrins (Kullander and Klein, 2002).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Kullander and Klein, 2002.

claim: Deregulation of the Eph/ephrin system contributes to the pathogenesis of many types of cancer, including GBM.
source: Deregulation of the Eph/ephrin system contributes to the pathogenesis of many types of cancer, including GBM (Pasquale, 2010).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Pasquale, 2010.

claim: EphA2 and EphA3 drive GSC self-renewal.
source: Indeed, EphA2 and EphA3 were shown to drive GSC self-renewal, whereas EphA2, EphA4, EphB2, ephrin-B2 and ephrin-B3 have all been linked to GBM invasion, through incompletely understood mechanisms (Day et al., 2014; Tu et al., 2012; Binda et al., 2012; Day et al., 2013; Nakada et al., 2010; 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Day et al., 2014; Tu et al., 2012; Binda et al., 2012; Day et al., 2013; Nakada et al., 2010; 2011.

claim: EphA2, EphA4, EphB2, ephrin-B2 and ephrin-B3 have all been linked to GBM invasion.
source: Indeed, EphA2 and EphA3 were shown to drive GSC self-renewal, whereas EphA2, EphA4, EphB2, ephrin-B2 and ephrin-B3 have all been linked to GBM invasion, through incompletely understood mechanisms (Day et al., 2014; Tu et al., 2012; Binda et al., 2012; Day et al., 2013; Nakada et al., 2010; 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Day et al., 2014; Tu et al., 2012; Binda et al., 2012; Day et al., 2013; Nakada et al., 2010; 2011.

claim: Transformation to GSC-like cells overrides the tumour-suppressive mechanism of endothelial ephrin-B2 to drive perivascular invasion.
source: We found that ephrin-B2 expressed on vascular endothelial cells inhibits the migration of non-tumourigenic cells, resulting in cell confinement. In contrast, transformation to GSC-like cells overrides this tumour-suppressive mechanism to drive perivascular invasion.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by the experimental data in the manuscript.

claim: Upregulation of ephrin-B2 in GSC-like cells desensitizes the cells to vascular confinement by constitutively activating Eph forward signalling non-cell-autonomously.
source: We show that this is caused by upregulation in GSC-like cells of the same ephrin-B2 ligand, which desensitizes the cells to vascular confinement by constitutively activating Eph forward signalling non-cell-autonomously.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by the experimental data in Figure 3.

claim: Ephrin-B2 reverse signaling elicits tumour cell proliferation in the absence of normal anchorage signals by driving Rho-A-dependent cytokinesis in a cell-autonomous manner.
source: Furthermore, we discovered that ephrin-B2 reverse signaling also elicits tumour cell proliferation in the absence of normal anchorage signals by driving Rho-A-dependent cytokinesis in a cell-autonomous manner.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by the experimental data in Figures 4 and 5.

claim: Ephrin-B2 overexpression is sufficient to fully transform immortalised NSC to the same extent as oncogenic Ras.
source: Consistent with these important roles, ephrin-B2 overexpression was sufficient to fully transform immortalised NSC to the same extent as oncogenic Ras.
evidence: This is supported by tumourigenicity studies shown in Figure 4.

claim: High Ephrin-B2 levels are detected in perivascular tumour cells with GSC features at the infiltrative tumour margin in human GBM specimens.
source: In human GBM specimens, high Ephrin-B2 levels were detected in perivascular tumour cells with GSC features at the infiltrative tumour margin, indicative of a role in the GSC compartment in primary tumours.
evidence: This is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 6a.

claim: GSC1 and GSC2 retained stem cell properties in vitro as judged by high clonal efficiency in neurosphere culture and differentiation into glial and neuronal lineages upon mitogen withdrawal.
source: In contrast, GSC1 and GSC2 retained stem cell properties in vitro as judged by high clonal efficiency in neurosphere culture and differentiation into glial and neuronal lineages upon mitogen withdrawal (Figure 1—figure supplement 1a–c).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1a–c.

claim: GSC1 and GSC2 formed colonies in soft agar.
source: Furthermore, both cell types (but not their immortalised controls) formed colonies in soft agar (Figure 4c,d) and gave rise to highly aggressive tumours upon intracranial transplantation in immunocompromised mice (5/5 animals, 100% penetrance, median survival 24d for GSC1 and 38.5 for GSC2), whereas GSC1 also did so in syngeneic animals (5/9 animals, 56% penetrance, median survival 73d), indicative of a more aggressive phenotype.
evidence: This is supported by soft agar assay data shown in Figure 4c,d.

claim: GSC1 gave rise to highly aggressive tumours upon intracranial transplantation in immunocompromised mice with 100% penetrance and median survival of 24 days.
source: Furthermore, both cell types (but not their immortalised controls) formed colonies in soft agar (Figure 4c,d) and gave rise to highly aggressive tumours upon intracranial transplantation in immunocompromised mice (5/5 animals, 100% penetrance, median survival 24d for GSC1 and 38.5 for GSC2), whereas GSC1 also did so in syngeneic animals (5/9 animals, 56% penetrance, median survival 73d), indicative of a more aggressive phenotype.
evidence: This is supported by in vivo tumourigenicity data.

claim: GSC2 gave rise to highly aggressive tumours upon intracranial transplantation in immunocompromised mice with 100% penetrance and median survival of 38.5 days.
source: Furthermore, both cell types (but not their immortalised controls) formed colonies in soft agar (Figure 4c,d) and gave rise to highly aggressive tumours upon intracranial transplantation in immunocompromised mice (5/5 animals, 100% penetrance, median survival 24d for GSC1 and 38.5 for GSC2), whereas GSC1 also did so in syngeneic animals (5/9 animals, 56% penetrance, median survival 73d), indicative of a more aggressive phenotype.
evidence: This is supported by in vivo tumourigenicity data.

claim: GSC1 formed tumours in syngeneic animals with 56% penetrance and median survival of 73 days.
source: Furthermore, both cell types (but not their immortalised controls) formed colonies in soft agar (Figure 4c,d) and gave rise to highly aggressive tumours upon intracranial transplantation in immunocompromised mice (5/5 animals, 100% penetrance, median survival 24d for GSC1 and 38.5 for GSC2), whereas GSC1 also did so in syngeneic animals (5/9 animals, 56% penetrance, median survival 73d), indicative of a more aggressive phenotype.
evidence: This is supported by in vivo tumourigenicity data.

claim: As little as 100 cells of either GSC1 or GSC2 line was sufficient to generate aggressive tumours.
source: Consistent with their stem-like properties, clonal dilution experiments revealed that as little as 100 cells of either line was sufficient to generate aggressive tumours (Figure 1—figure supplement 1d).
evidence: This is supported by limiting dilution analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1d.

claim: GSC1 and GSC2 tumours recapitulated the histopathology and gene expression signatures of human GBM, including presence of necrosis, neovascularization, nestin and Sox2 expression.
source: Importantly, the tumours recapitulated the histopathology and gene expression signatures of human GBM, including presence of necrosis, neovascularization, nestin and Sox2 expression and a strong enrichment in the Verhaak mesenchymal subtype gene signature (Figure 1a–d and Figure 1—figure supplement 1e) (Kleihues, 2000; Verhaak et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by histopathology and gene expression data shown in Figure 1a–d and Figure 1—figure supplement 1e.

claim: GSC1 and GSC2 tumours showed strong enrichment in the Verhaak mesenchymal subtype gene signature.
source: Importantly, the tumours recapitulated the histopathology and gene expression signatures of human GBM, including presence of necrosis, neovascularization, nestin and Sox2 expression and a strong enrichment in the Verhaak mesenchymal subtype gene signature (Figure 1a–d and Figure 1—figure supplement 1e) (Kleihues, 2000; Verhaak et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by gene expression analysis shown in Figure 1c,d.

claim: The majority of invading GSC1 and GSC2 cells migrated along blood vessels and displaced astrocyte endfeet and pericytes to come in direct contact with endothelial cells.
source: The tumours presented diffuse borders with the majority of invading cells migrating along blood vessels and displacing astrocyte endfeet and pericytes to come in direct contact with endothelial cells, as previously reported for both murine and human GSC (Figure 1b and Figure 1—figure supplement 1f) (Zagzag et al., 2008; Farin et al., 2006; Nagano et al., 1993; Watkins et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 1b and Figure 1—figure supplement 1f, and citations to Zagzag et al., 2008; Farin et al., 2006; Nagano et al., 1993; Watkins et al., 2014.

claim: Individual GSC1 migrated out of the tumour mass along blood vessels, resulting in cell scattering, while imNSC remained in stationary groups.
source: However, while individual GSC1 migrated out of the tumour mass along blood vessels, resulting in cell scattering, imNSC remained in stationary groups (Figure 1e,f).
evidence: This is supported by intravital imaging data shown in Figure 1e,f.

claim: GSC1 perivascular migration was independent of their position relative to the tumour bulk or cell density.
source: GSC1 perivascular migration was independent of their position relative to the tumour bulk or cell density, with single cells migrating from the main tumour as efficiently and at similar speed as GSC1 migrating at a distance from the tumour margin (Figure 1e and Figure 1—figure supplement 1h).
evidence: This is supported by intravital imaging data shown in Figure 1e and Figure 1—figure supplement 1h.

claim: Signals from the vasculature compartmentalise non-tumourigenic cells to restrict their migration, whereas transformation overrides these signals to enable perivascular spread.
source: This suggests that signals from the vasculature compartmentalises non-tumourigenic cells to restrict their migration, whereas transformation overrides these signals to enable perivascular spread.
evidence: This is an inference based on the intravital imaging observations.

claim: Endothelial cells strongly repelled and compartmentalised imNSC forming a sharp boundary in vitro.
source: Remarkably, this assay closely recapitulated in vivo migratory patterns, in that endothelial cells strongly repelled and compartmentalised imNSC forming a sharp boundary (Figure 1 and Video 1).
evidence: This is supported by in vitro migration assay data shown in Figure 1g and Video 1.

claim: GSC1 were refractory to compartmentalisation and migrated over the endothelial monolayer.
source: In contrast, GSC1 were refractory to compartmentalisation and migrated over the endothelial monolayer, giving rise to an uneven and longer boundary (Figure 1g and Video 2).
evidence: This is supported by in vitro migration assay data shown in Figure 1g and Video 2.

claim: Ephrin-B2-Fc compartmentalised imNSCs, but not GSC.
source: As shown in Figure 1i and Videos 3 and 4, ephrin-B2-Fc compartmentalised imNSCs, but not GSC, to the same extent as endothelial cells.
evidence: This is supported by in vitro migration assay data shown in Figure 1i and Videos 3 and 4.

claim: Efnb2 knock-down in endothelial cells disrupted boundary formation against imNSC.
source: Conversely, Efnb2 knock-down in endothelial cells disrupted boundary formation against imNSC, indicating that endothelial ephrin-B2 is both necessary and sufficient for compartmentalisation (Figure 1j and Figure 1—figure supplement 1j).
evidence: This is supported by in vitro migration assay data shown in Figure 1j and Figure 1—figure supplement 1j.

claim: Endothelial ephrin-B2 is both necessary and sufficient for compartmentalisation of imNSC.
source: Conversely, Efnb2 knock-down in endothelial cells disrupted boundary formation against imNSC, indicating that endothelial ephrin-B2 is both necessary and sufficient for compartmentalisation (Figure 1j and Figure 1—figure supplement 1j).
evidence: This is an inference based on the Efnb2 knock-down and ephrin-B2-Fc experiments.

claim: Selective deletion of ephrin-B2 in the endothelium elicited robust perivascular migration of imNSC1 in vivo.
source: Strikingly, selective deletion of ephrin-B2 in the endothelium elicited robust perivascular migration of imNSC1, confirming that vascular ephrin-B2 compartmentalises non-tumourigenic cells in vivo (Figure 1e,f).
evidence: This is supported by intravital imaging data in endothelial-specific Efnb2 knockout mice shown in Figure 1e,f.

claim: Vascular ephrin-B2 compartmentalises non-tumourigenic cells in vivo.
source: Strikingly, selective deletion of ephrin-B2 in the endothelium elicited robust perivascular migration of imNSC1, confirming that vascular ephrin-B2 compartmentalises non-tumourigenic cells in vivo (Figure 1e,f).
evidence: This is confirmed by the intravital imaging experiments in endothelial-specific Efnb2 knockout mice.

claim: Elevated Ras signalling strongly downregulated Epha4, Ephb1 and Ephb2 and upregulated Efna5 and Efnb2 in both GSC1 and GSC2 models.
source: We found that p53 and Rb inactivation did not change Eph/ephrin expression substantially. In contrast, elevated Ras signalling, triggered by either RasV12 expression or Nf1 loss, strongly downregulated three Ephs (Epha4, Ephb1 and Ephb2) and upregulated two ephrins (Efna5 and Efnb2) in both models.
evidence: This is supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 2a and Figure 2—figure supplement 1a.

claim: Of the Eph/ephrin genes that changed with Ras signaling, only Ephb1, Ephb2 and Efnb2 changed significantly at the protein level.
source: However, western analysis indicated that of these genes, only Ephb1, Ephb2 and Efnb2 changed significantly at the protein level (Figure 2b) and were thus further assessed in migration assays against ephrin-B2-Fc.
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 2b.

claim: Re-introduction of Ephb1 or Ephb2 by overexpression in GSC1 did not affect migration towards recombinant ephrin-B2-Fc.
source: Surprisingly, we found that re-introduction of Ephb1 or Ephb2 by overexpression in GSC1 (Figure 2—figure supplement 1b) did not affect migration towards recombinant ephrin-B2-Fc, indicating that changes in the complement of Eph receptors do not underlie unimpeded migration, as in other systems (Figure 2c) (Astin et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by migration assay data shown in Figure 2c and Figure 2—figure supplement 1b.

claim: Genetic deletion of Efnb2 in GSC1 fully rescued boundary formation in response to ephrin-B2-Fc and endothelial cells in vitro and blocked perivascular migration in vivo.
source: Instead, genetic deletion of Efnb2 in GSC1 (Figure 2—figure supplement 1c) fully rescued boundary formation in response to ephrin-B2-Fc and endothelial cells in vitro and blocked perivascular migration in vivo (Figure 2c–e).
evidence: This is supported by migration assay and intravital imaging data shown in Figure 2c–e.

claim: Efnb2 overexpression conferred imNSC1 with the ability to migrate over recombinant ephrin-B2 and a cultured endothelium and to escape vascular compartmentalisation in vivo.
source: Conversely, Efnb2 overexpression (Figure 2—figure supplement 1d) conferred imNSC1 with the ability to migrate over recombinant ephrin-B2 and a cultured endothelium and to escape vascular compartmentalisation in vivo (Figure 2c–e).
evidence: This is supported by migration assay and intravital imaging data shown in Figure 2c–e.

claim: Ephrin-B2 upregulation downstream of Ras underlies GSC evasion of ephrin-B2-mediated endothelial repulsion and invasion along the vasculature.
source: Together, these results show that ephrin-B2 upregulation downstream of Ras underlies GSC evasion of ephrin-B2-mediated endothelial repulsion and invasion along the vasculature.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the genetic manipulation experiments in Figure 2.

claim: Approximately 20% of GSC cells are repelled on first contact with ephrin-B2-Fc.
source: We noticed that, although all GSC cells eventually migrated over ephrin-B2-Fc, a proportion of the cells (~20%) are repelled on first contact (Figure 3a).
evidence: This is supported by quantification of cell behavior shown in Figure 3a.

claim: Repelled GSC cells invariably migrated towards ephrin-B2-Fc either as single cells or in small groups (<2 contacts), whereas non-repelled cells migrated in larger groups (>3 contacts).
source: Repelled cells invariably migrated towards ephrin-B2-Fc either as single cells or in small groups (<2 contacts), whereas non-repelled cells migrated in larger groups (>3 contacts) (Figure 3b).
evidence: This is supported by quantification of homotypic cell-cell contacts shown in Figure 3b.

claim: Homotypic cell-cell interactions among GSC, mediated by intrinsic ephrin-B2, underpin evasion of extrinsic ephrin-B2 repulsion.
source: This suggested that homotypic cell-cell interactions among GSC, mediated by intrinsic ephrin-B2, might underpin evasion of extrinsic ephrin-B2 repulsion.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that non-repelled cells migrate in larger groups.

claim: Both culture in low Ca2+ media and dominant-negative N-cadherin overexpression completely disrupted cell-cell junctions without affecting cell motility and blocked GSC migration over ephrin-B2 ligands.
source: Both culture in low Ca2+ media and dominant-negative N-cadherin overexpression completely disrupted cell-cell junctions without affecting cell motility (Figure 3—figure supplement 1a,b) and blocked GSC migration over ephrin-B2 ligands, indicating that homotypic cell-cell interactions are specifically required (Figure 3c).
evidence: This is supported by migration assay data shown in Figure 3c and Figure 3—figure supplement 1a,b.

claim: Homotypic cell-cell interactions are specifically required for GSC migration over ephrin-B2 ligands.
source: Both culture in low Ca2+ media and dominant-negative N-cadherin overexpression completely disrupted cell-cell junctions without affecting cell motility (Figure 3—figure supplement 1a,b) and blocked GSC migration over ephrin-B2 ligands, indicating that homotypic cell-cell interactions are specifically required (Figure 3c).
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experiments disrupting cell-cell junctions.

claim: Ectopic expression of a C-terminal truncated form of ephrin-B2 (ΔCEfnb2), which lacks reverse signalling, promoted imNSC migration over ephrin-B2-Fc to the same extent as full-length Efnb2.
source: Ectopic expression of a C-terminal truncated form of ephrin-B2 (ΔCEfnb2), which lacks reverse signalling (Pfaff et al., 2008), promoted imNSC migration over ephrin-B2-Fc to the same extent as full-length Efnb2, demonstrating that forward signalling between neighboring cells is responsible (Figure 3d and Figure 2—figure supplement 1d).
evidence: This is supported by migration assay data shown in Figure 3d.

claim: Forward signalling between neighboring cells is responsible for ephrin-B2-mediated migration over ephrin-B2-Fc.
source: Ectopic expression of a C-terminal truncated form of ephrin-B2 (ΔCEfnb2), which lacks reverse signalling (Pfaff et al., 2008), promoted imNSC migration over ephrin-B2-Fc to the same extent as full-length Efnb2, demonstrating that forward signalling between neighboring cells is responsible (Figure 3d and Figure 2—figure supplement 1d).
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the ΔCEfnb2 experiment.

claim: GSC exhibited constitutively high levels of activated Eph receptors (p-Eph), despite their reduced levels of EphB1 and EphB2.
source: Indeed, western analysis (Figure 3e) indicated that while imNSC controls displayed low basal levels of activated Eph receptors (p-Eph), GSC exhinited constitutively high levels of p-Eph, despite their reduced levels of EphB1 and EphB2 (Figure 2b) and no increase in other ephrin-B2 receptors in these cells (Figure 2a and not shown).
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 3e.

claim: High basal p-Eph in GSC could be mimicked by ephrin-B2 overexpression in imNSC and reduced to basal control levels by culture in low Ca2+.
source: High basal p-Eph could be mimicked by ephrin-B2 overexpression in imNSC and reduced to basal control levels by culture in low Ca2+ (Figure 3e).
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 3e.

claim: Co-culture with endothelial cells or treatment with recombinant ephrin-B2 failed to further activate Eph receptors in GSC.
source: In addition, the high phosphorylation levels of Ephs in GSC appeared to be saturating, as, in contrast to imNSC, co-culture with endothelial cells or treatment with recombinant ephrin-B2 failed to further activate Eph receptors in these cells (Figure 3f).
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 3f.

claim: Eph desensitization in GSC was entirely dependent on endogenous ephrin-B2 because genetic deletion of Efnb2 in GSC fully restored Eph stimulation by exogenous ephrin-B2.
source: Importantly, Eph desensitization was again entirely dependent on endogenous ephrin-B2 because genetic deletion of Efnb2 in GSC fully restored Eph stimulation by exogenous ephrin-B2.
evidence: This is supported by western blot data showing restored Eph activation in GSC1 Efnb2-/- cells.

claim: High basal levels of activated Eph resulted in GSC undergoing much greater scattering and faster migration than imNSC following homotypic collisions in sparse monocultures, in an ephrin-B2-dependent manner.
source: Consistent with the known ability of Ephs to trigger repulsion (Astin et al., 2010; Pasquale, 2010), such high basal levels of activated Eph resulted in GSC undergoing much greater scattering and faster migration than imNSC following homotypic collisions in sparse monocultures, in an ephrin-B2-dependent manner (Figure 3—figure supplement 1c,d).
evidence: This is supported by cell tracking data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1c,d.

claim: Ephrin-B2-Fc pretreatment enabled imNSC migration over the ephrin-B2 boundary.
source: Remarkably, we found that ephrin-B2-Fc (but not Fc) pretreatment enabled migration over the ephrin-B2 boundary, confirming that activation of Eph forward signaling on first contact with exogenous ephrin-B2 is the mechanism involved.
evidence: This is supported by migration assay data shown in Figure 3g.

claim: Activation of Eph forward signaling on first contact with exogenous ephrin-B2 is the mechanism by which GSC override ephrin-B2-mediated repulsion.
source: Remarkably, we found that ephrin-B2-Fc (but not Fc) pretreatment enabled migration over the ephrin-B2 boundary, confirming that activation of Eph forward signaling on first contact with exogenous ephrin-B2 is the mechanism involved.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the ephrin-B2-Fc pretreatment experiment.

claim: High pEph levels were detected in cells migrating along blood vessels at the tumour edge in GSC1-derived orthotopic tumours.
source: In agreement with these findings, immunofluorescence analysis of GSC1-derived orthotopic tumours revealed high pEph levels in cells migrating along blood vessels at the tumour edge, indicating that constitutive forward signaling also contributes to perivascular invasion in vivo (Figure 3—figure supplement 1e).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1e.

claim: GSC escape from endothelial compartmentalisation depends on continuous activation of Eph forward signalling elicited by elevated ephrin-B2 through homotypic cell-cell interactions within the tumour cell population.
source: We conclude that GSC escape from endothelial compartmentalisation depends on continuous activation of Eph forward signalling elicited by elevated ephrin-B2 through homotypic cell-cell interactions within the tumour cell population.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the collective findings in Figure 3.

claim: ImNSC1 did not form tumours while GSC1 formed tumours at full penetrance in nude mice.
source: Strikingly, quantitative imaging and survival analysis revealed that, while imNSC1 did not form tumours and GSC1 formed tumours at full penetrance, Efnb2 deletion strongly suppressed GSC1 tumour growth and, conversely, Efnb2 overexpression was sufficient to fully transform imNSC (Figure 4a,b).
evidence: This is supported by in vivo tumourigenicity data shown in Figure 4a,b.

claim: Efnb2 deletion strongly suppressed GSC1 tumour growth in nude mice.
source: Strikingly, quantitative imaging and survival analysis revealed that, while imNSC1 did not form tumours and GSC1 formed tumours at full penetrance, Efnb2 deletion strongly suppressed GSC1 tumour growth and, conversely, Efnb2 overexpression was sufficient to fully transform imNSC (Figure 4a,b).
evidence: This is supported by in vivo tumourigenicity data shown in Figure 4a,b.

claim: Efnb2 overexpression was sufficient to fully transform imNSC in nude mice.
source: Strikingly, quantitative imaging and survival analysis revealed that, while imNSC1 did not form tumours and GSC1 formed tumours at full penetrance, Efnb2 deletion strongly suppressed GSC1 tumour growth and, conversely, Efnb2 overexpression was sufficient to fully transform imNSC (Figure 4a,b).
evidence: This is supported by in vivo tumourigenicity data shown in Figure 4a,b.

claim: ImNSC1-Efnb2 tumours resulted in a similar median survival as GSC1 (28 days).
source: Specifically, imNSC1-Efnb2 tumours resulted in a similar median survival as GSC1 (28d).
evidence: This is supported by survival analysis data shown in Figure 4b.

claim: All imNSC animals survived tumour-free beyond 200 days.
source: In contrast, all imNSC animals survived tumour-free beyond 200 days and 7 out of 9 animals of the GSC1Efnb2-/-cohort developed lesions with much slower kinetics, while the remaining 2 mice remained tumour-free, as confirmed by post-mortem examination.
evidence: This is supported by survival analysis data shown in Figure 4b.

claim: 7 out of 9 animals of the GSC1Efnb2-/- cohort developed lesions with much slower kinetics, while the remaining 2 mice remained tumour-free.
source: In contrast, all imNSC animals survived tumour-free beyond 200 days and 7 out of 9 animals of the GSC1Efnb2-/-cohort developed lesions with much slower kinetics, while the remaining 2 mice remained tumour-free, as confirmed by post-mortem examination.
evidence: This is supported by survival analysis data shown in Figure 4b.

claim: Ephrin-B2 can substitute oncogenic Ras for transformation.
source: Thus, ephrin-B2 can substitute oncogenic Ras for transformation.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the tumourigenicity studies showing that Efnb2 overexpression transforms imNSC.

claim: ImNSC1-Efnb2 and GSC1 formed large colonies in soft agar at similar high efficiency.
source: Instead, imNSC1-Efnb2 and GSC1 formed large colonies at similar high efficiency, indicating that ephrin-B2 drives anchorage-independent proliferation.
evidence: This is supported by soft agar assay data shown in Figure 4c.

claim: Ephrin-B2 drives anchorage-independent proliferation.
source: Instead, imNSC1-Efnb2 and GSC1 formed large colonies at similar high efficiency, indicating that ephrin-B2 drives anchorage-independent proliferation.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the soft agar assay results.

claim: Ephrin-B2 effects on proliferation were dependent on reverse signalling and independent of homotypic cell-cell contact.
source: Intriguingly, and in contrast to its role in perivascular invasion, ephrin-B2 effects on proliferation were dependent on reverse signalling and independent of homotypic cell-cell contact.
evidence: This is supported by experiments with ΔCEfnb2 and DN-Ncadherin shown in Figure 4c and Figure 4—figure supplement 1a.

claim: ImNSC1-ΔCEfnb2 did not form colonies in suspension.
source: Indeed, imNSC1-ΔCEfnb2 did not form colonies in suspension and imNSC1-Efnb2 overexpressing DN-Ncadherin formed colonies at similar efficiency as GFP-controls, demonstrating that Eph forward signalling is dispensable (Figure 4c and Figure 4—figure supplement 1a).
evidence: This is supported by soft agar assay data shown in Figure 4c.

claim: ImNSC1-Efnb2 overexpressing DN-Ncadherin formed colonies at similar efficiency as GFP-controls.
source: Indeed, imNSC1-ΔCEfnb2 did not form colonies in suspension and imNSC1-Efnb2 overexpressing DN-Ncadherin formed colonies at similar efficiency as GFP-controls, demonstrating that Eph forward signalling is dispensable (Figure 4c and Figure 4—figure supplement 1a).
evidence: This is supported by soft agar assay data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1a.

claim: Eph forward signalling is dispensable for ephrin-B2-mediated anchorage-independent proliferation.
source: Indeed, imNSC1-ΔCEfnb2 did not form colonies in suspension and imNSC1-Efnb2 overexpressing DN-Ncadherin formed colonies at similar efficiency as GFP-controls, demonstrating that Eph forward signalling is dispensable (Figure 4c and Figure 4—figure supplement 1a).
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the ΔCEfnb2 and DN-Ncadherin experiments.

claim: GSC1 continued to proliferate in methylcellulose with similar kinetics to attached cells, while suspended imNSC did not.
source: As anticipated, all cells proliferated efficiently in attachment (Figure 4e). By contrast, their behavior in suspension was very distinct. While GSC1 continued to proliferate in methylcellulose with similar kinetics, suspended imNSC did not.
evidence: This is supported by cell cycle analysis data shown in Figure 4e.

claim: ImNSC arrested with a 4n DNA content in suspension, indicating that their progression through G2/M is blocked by an anchorage checkpoint.
source: This was not due to cell death as judged by activated caspase3+ staining (Figure 4—figure supplement 1c). Instead, imNSC arrested with a 4n DNA content. This indicated that while imNSC progress normally through the G1 and S phases of the cell-cycle, their progression through G2/M is blocked by an anchorage checkpoint, which is overridden by activated Ras.
evidence: This is supported by cell cycle analysis data shown in Figure 4e.

claim: Ras-mediated progression through G2/M was dependent on ephrin-B2 reverse signalling.
source: Importantly, Ras-mediated progression through G2/M was again dependent on ephrin-B2 reverse signalling, because Efnb2 deletion in GSC re-instated the G2/M arrest (without additional apoptosis, Figure 4—figure supplement 1c), and the cell-cycle arrest of imNSC could be rescued by overexpression of full-length, but not ΔC, Efnb2 (Figure 4e).
evidence: This is supported by cell cycle analysis data shown in Figure 4e and Figure 4—figure supplement 1c.

claim: The cell-cycle profiles of imNSC1, imNSC1-Efnb2, GSC1 and GSC1Efnb2-/- recovered from injected brains were indistinguishable from the corresponding methylcellulose cultures.
source: Strikingly, the cell-cycle profiles of all cells were indistinguishable from the corresponding methylcellulose cultures, confirming that ephrin-B2 drives gliomagenesis in vivo by promoting proliferation in the absence of normal anchorage signals.
evidence: This is supported by cell cycle analysis data shown in Figure 4f.

claim: Ephrin-B2 drives gliomagenesis in vivo by promoting proliferation in the absence of normal anchorage signals.
source: Strikingly, the cell-cycle profiles of all cells were indistinguishable from the corresponding methylcellulose cultures, confirming that ephrin-B2 drives gliomagenesis in vivo by promoting proliferation in the absence of normal anchorage signals.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the comparison of cell cycle profiles in vitro and in vivo.

claim: All methylcellulose cultures devoid of ephrin-B2 reverse signalling (imNSC1, imNSC1-ΔCEfnb2 and GSC1 Efnb2-/-) contained a much larger proportion of EdU- binucleated cells with decondensed chromatin compared to adherent conditions, indicative of a cytokinesis block.
source: As shown in Figure 5a and b, we found that all methylcellulose cultures devoid of ephrin-B2 reverse signalling (imNSC1, imNSC1-ΔCEfnb2 and GSC1 Efnb2-/-) contained a much larger proportion of EdU- binucleated cells with decondensed chromatin compared to adherent conditions, indicative of a cytokinesis block (Thullberg et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by binucleated cell quantification data shown in Figure 5a,b.

claim: Cells with intact ephrin-B2 reverse signalling (imNSC1-Efnb2 and GSC1) had similar low percentages of EdU+ binucleated cells in both suspension and attachment culture.
source: In contrast, cells with intact ephrin-B2 reverse signalling (imNSC1-Efnb2 and GSC1) had similar low percentages of EdU+ binucleated cells in both suspension and attachment culture.
evidence: This is supported by binucleated cell quantification data shown in Figure 5b.

claim: Ephrin-B2 reverse signalling drives anchorage-independent cytokinesis.
source: Thus, ephrin-B2 reverse signalling drives anchorage-independent cytokinesis.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the binucleated cell analysis.

claim: Levels of active RhoA were low in suspended cells that lacked ephrin-B2 reverse signalling but greatly increased in cells that express high levels of full-length ephrin-B2.
source: In stark contrast, levels of active RhoA were low in suspended cells that lacked ephrin-B2 reverse signalling (i.e. imNSC, imNSC1-ΔCEfnb2 and GSC1Efnb-/-) but greatly increased in cells that express high levels of full-length ephrin-B2 (i.e. imNSC1-Efnb2 and GSC1), suggesting the involvement of RhoA (Figure 5c).
evidence: This is supported by RhoA pull-down assay data shown in Figure 5c.

claim: RhoA-V14 could rescue the cell-cycle arrest of imNSC1 and GSC1Efnb2-/-.
source: Remarkably, RhoA-V14 could rescue the cell-cycle arrest of imNSC1 and GSC1Efnb2-/-, whereas RhoA-N19 arrested imNSC1-Efnb2 and GSC1 in G2/M (Figure 5d and Figure 5—figure supplement 1c).
evidence: This is supported by cell cycle analysis data shown in Figure 5d.

claim: RhoA-N19 arrested imNSC1-Efnb2 and GSC1 in G2/M.
source: Remarkably, RhoA-V14 could rescue the cell-cycle arrest of imNSC1 and GSC1Efnb2-/-, whereas RhoA-N19 arrested imNSC1-Efnb2 and GSC1 in G2/M (Figure 5d and Figure 5—figure supplement 1c).
evidence: This is supported by cell cycle analysis data shown in Figure 5d.

claim: Ephrin-B2 drives anchorage-independent cytokinesis of GSCs through RhoA-mediated reverse signalling.
source: Together, these results demonstrate that ephrin-B2 drives anchorage-independent cytokinesis of GSCs through RhoA-mediated reverse signalling.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the RhoA manipulation experiments.

claim: All 8 patient tumours presented cytoplasmic and membranous Ephrin-B2 expression in 25 to 90% of the tumour cells.
source: All tumours presented cytoplasmic and membranous Ephrin-B2 expression in 25 to 90% of the tumour cells, as well as neurons, inflammatory cells and vascular endothelial cells, as reported (Gale et al., 2001; Sawamiphak et al., 2010; Ottone et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 6a.

claim: ALDH1 expression was detected predominantly in neoplastic cells surrounding blood vessels, in perinecrotic regions and at the infiltrative tumour margin.
source: In contrast, ALDH1 expression was less abundant, with expression detected predominantly in neoplastic cells surrounding blood vessels, in perinecrotic regions and at the infiltrative tumour margin, as expected from a stem cell marker (Rasper et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 6a.

claim: Many perivascular ALDH1+ neoplastic cells at the infiltrative tumour margin co-expressed ephrin-B2.
source: Importantly, many perivascular ALDH1+ neoplastic cells at the infiltrative tumour margin co-expressed ephrin-B2.
evidence: This is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 6a.

claim: Ephrin-B2 is expressed in stem-like cells invading along blood vessels in primary human tumours.
source: Thus, ephrin-B2 is expressed in stem-like cells invading along blood vessels in primary human tumours.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the co-expression of ephrin-B2 and ALDH1 in perivascular cells.

claim: There is a significant correlation between EFNB2 and mesenchymal gene expression levels in primary human GSC lines.
source: Consistent with our mouse models, RNA-sequencing analysis revealed frequent upregulation of EFNB2 in GSCs and a significant correlation between EFNB2 and mesenchymal gene expression levels (Figure 6b).
evidence: This is supported by RNA-sequencing analysis shown in Figure 6b.

claim: EFNB2 expression levels are highest in mesenchymal and classical GBM subtypes in the TCGA dataset.
source: In addition, analysis of 402 GBM from the TGCA dataset classified according to Verhaak et al. and corrected for IDH1 status, indicated that EFNB2 expression levels are highest in mesenchymal and classical GBM subtypes (Figure 6—figure supplement 1c) (Verhaak et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by TCGA data analysis shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1c.

claim: EFNB2 correlated with decreased survival in mesenchymal GBM.
source: When tumours were divided into two groups on the basis of EFNB2 levels relative to median expression within subtypes, EFNB2 correlated with decreased survival in mesenchymal GBM (Figure 6—figure supplement 1d).
evidence: This is supported by Kaplan-Meier analysis shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1d.

claim: In the absence of ephrin-B2, human GSC lost the ability to migrate over coated ephrin-B2.
source: As shown in Figure 6c–h, we found that, similar to the murine GSC models, in the absence of ephrin-B2, GSC (but not SCR shRNA-transduced controls) lost the ability to migrate over coated ephrin-B2 and failed to proliferate anchorage-independently, resulting in a G2/M cell-cycle arrest.
evidence: This is supported by migration assay data shown in Figure 6c.

claim: In the absence of ephrin-B2, human GSC failed to proliferate anchorage-independently, resulting in a G2/M cell-cycle arrest.
source: As shown in Figure 6c–h, we found that, similar to the murine GSC models, in the absence of ephrin-B2, GSC (but not SCR shRNA-transduced controls) lost the ability to migrate over coated ephrin-B2 and failed to proliferate anchorage-independently, resulting in a G2/M cell-cycle arrest.
evidence: This is supported by soft agar and cell cycle analysis data shown in Figure 6d,e.

claim: EFNB2 knock-down cells gave rise to slower growing tumours in only 2 out of 10 animals, with the other 8 mice remaining tumour-free for >1 year.
source: We found a dramatic impairment of tumour growth in the EFNB2 knock-down group relative to control, in that vector-transduced G26 formed GBM in all animals (as previously reported (Stricker et al., 2012) whilst EFNB2 knock-down cells gave rise to slower growing tumours in only 2 out of 10 animals, with the other 8 mice remaining tumour-free for >1 year.
evidence: This is supported by in vivo tumourigenicity data shown in Figure 7a-c.

claim: Vascular contact was severely compromised in EFNB2 knock-down cells at 10 days following implantation.
source: SCR GSC associated with the vasculature at this early time point (and at later stages of tumour growth), resulting in vascular co-option, as reported (Figure 7d and Figure 7—figure supplement 1) (Watkins et al., 2014). In contrast, vascular contact was severely compromised in knock-down cells.
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 7d.

claim: EFNB2 downregulation resulted in a marked decrease in proliferation, accompanied by an arrest in the G2/M phase of the cell-cycle in vivo.
source: Furthermore, similar to GSC1Efnb2-/- murine cells, EFNB2 downregulation resulted in a marked decrease in proliferation, accompanied by an arrest in the G2/M phase of the cell-cycle, indicative of a cytokinesis block (Figure 7e,f).
evidence: This is supported by Ki67 staining and cell cycle analysis data shown in Figure 7e,f.

claim: Ephrin-B2 drives tumour initiation by mediating vascular association and proliferation of human GSC.
source: Thus, Ephrin-B2 drives tumour initiation by mediating vascular association and proliferation of human GSC.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the in vivo experiments with EFNB2 knock-down human GSC.

claim: B11 strongly suppressed tumour growth in all animals without any evidence of toxicity, with three of six animals showing complete regression.
source: Remarkably, B11 strongly suppressed tumour growth in all animals without any evidence of toxicity, with three of six animals showing complete regression, as judged by quantitative bioluminescence imaging, survival analysis and post-mortem examination of the injected brains (Figure 8a–c).
evidence: This is supported by in vivo treatment data shown in Figure 8a-c.

claim: In B11-treated tumours, invading tumour cells failed to associate with and coopt the vasculature.
source: Analysis and quantification of the tumours immediately following treatment also revealed that, in contrast to vehicle-treated control tumours, invading tumour cells failed to associate with and coopt the vasculature (Figure 8d).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 8d.

claim: Proliferation was reduced in B11 tumours relative to controls, with B11 samples containing many Ki67+ multinucleated cells, indicative of a cytokinesis defect.
source: Furthermore, proliferation was reduced in B11 tumours relative to controls, with B11 samples containing many Ki67+ multinucleated cells, indicative of a cytokinesis defect (Figure 8e).
evidence: This is supported by Ki67 staining data shown in Figure 8e.

claim: B11 suppresses G26 tumourigenicity through inhibition of ephrin-B2-dependent perivascular invasion and anchorage-independent proliferation, independent of angiogenesis.
source: Therefore, B11 suppresses G26 tumourigenicity through inhibition of ephrin-B2-dependent perivascular invasion and anchorage-independent proliferation, independent of angiogenesis.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the B11 treatment experiments.

claim: Ephrin-B2 plays an important role in the pathogenesis of human GBM and its inhibition might be an effective strategy for curtailing GBM progression and recurrence.
source: We conclude that Ephrin-B2 plays an important role in the pathogenesis of human GBM and its inhibition might be an effective strategy for curtailing GBM progression and recurrence.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the collective findings with human GSC.
